meta.title: Responsible Generative Media
meta.thesis: Responsible Generative Media is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A campaign uses generated people and product scenes while needing consent, labels, and provenance. By the end, they should be able to build or review responsible-media release checklist with provenance and review owners, measure assets shipped with documented rights and disclosure status, and catch the failure where an image resembles a real person without consent or provenance.

mentalMap.title: Responsible Generative Media: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Govern synthetic images, speech, video, and music with intent, provenance, consent, review, and release records.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Responsible generative media treats every synthetic asset as a product artifact with provenance, consent, quality, and harm checks.

modules.title: Synthetic media changes audience trust
modules.sub: The first question is what viewers may believe.
modules.summary: Generated media must be judged by trust impact, not only aesthetics.

blocks.title: The risk starts with interpretation

spans.text: Problem anchor: a course team generates a teacher voiceover and a realistic image of a student using lab equipment. Learners may assume the voice is a real instructor and the image documents a real lab. Responsible media begins by asking what the audience will reasonably believe.
Low-risk abstract icons need lighter review than realistic people, public figures, medical scenes, political content, or identity-like voices.

blocks.analogy: Synthetic media needs a trust label, not just a beauty score.

spans.text: A release note says: synthetic narration, no real instructor likeness, script v3 approved, pronunciation checked, captions available, and rollback owner named. That is a governed asset, not an anonymous audio file.

blocks.title: Trust risk
blocks.prompt: Which asset needs the strongest review?

options.text: A realistic synthetic video of a real person explaining policy.
A non-human icon with no claims.

blocks.explanation: Realistic identity-like media carries higher trust and consent risk.

modules.title: Provenance and labels travel with the asset
modules.summary: Responsible workflows record how media was made and edited.
objectives: Use content credentials as one approach.

spans.text: C2PA provides an open standard for content provenance and authenticity. In a product workflow, provenance records model/tool, prompt or source, generation date, edits, reviewer, and synthetic status. Visible labels still matter because metadata may not display everywhere.

cells.text: history can be stripped or hidden

modules.title: Consent, likeness, and bias need preflight rules
modules.sub: Some media should not be generated without permission or policy.
modules.summary: Review people, voices, groups, and sensitive contexts before generation.

spans.text: Preflight asks whether the asset depicts a real person, imitates a voice, represents a protected group, makes a factual claim, or appears in a sensitive domain. If yes, require consent, stricter review, or a non-realistic alternative.

items.text: Use abstract avatars instead of fake students for sensitive scenarios.
Do not clone a teacher voice without permission and disclosure.
Do not use generated images as evidence that an event happened.
Review demographic representation when generating groups.

modules.title: Code a media release checklist
modules.summary: A small policy check catches missing provenance, consent, and review fields.

blocks.title: Synthetic media release-gate validator
blocks.code:
asset = {
    "id": "lesson-narration-03",
    "synthetic": True,
    "media_type": "audio",
    "model": "tts-model-x",
    "visible_label": "Synthetic narration",
    "likeness_consent": "not_applicable",
    "reviewer": "media-policy-owner",
    "factual_review": True,
    "provenance_recorded": True,
}
required = ["model", "visible_label", "likeness_consent", "reviewer"]
missing = [field for field in required if not asset.get(field)]
if asset["synthetic"] and not asset["provenance_recorded"]:
    missing.append("provenance_recorded")
print("release ok" if not missing else {"missing": missing})

spans.text: This toy gate makes omissions fail loudly before publishing.

predictThenReveal.prompt: What happens if visible_label is empty?
predictThenReveal.answer: The validator reports visible_label as missing. Synthetic media that affects trust needs disclosure.

spans.text: Checklist: synthetic status recorded; model/source and edits logged; visible label chosen; consent/likeness status clear; bias/factual review complete; rollback owner named.

modules.title: Release logs make media accountable
modules.summary: Responsible media needs owners, audit trails, takedown paths, and improvement loops.

blocks.title: A release record explains the choice later

spans.text: The log should include asset ID, lesson ID, synthetic status, generation source, edits, credentials/metadata, reviewer, policy version, approval decision, and takedown trigger. User reports can then lead to inspection, removal, or policy updates.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Publish synthetic media only with provenance, disclosure, review, and rollback ownership.
blocks.useWhen: Use this gate for realistic images, voices, videos, music, educational diagrams, and media that could be mistaken for evidence.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid publishing when consent is unclear, factual review is incomplete, or ownership is missing.

diffusion.label: Diffusion
diffusion.laymanDefinition: A generative process that learns to turn noise into structured media.
diffusion.technicalNote: Diffusion systems combine denoising steps, conditioning, schedulers, and safety controls; quality and provenance depend on the full pipeline.

latent_space.label: Latent space
latent_space.laymanDefinition: A compressed representation where models manipulate meaning more efficiently than raw pixels or audio.
latent_space.technicalNote: Latent-space choices affect speed, detail, editability, artifacts, and what safety or provenance checks can inspect.

pipeline.label: Pipeline
pipeline.laymanDefinition: The ordered set of model, preprocessing, generation, postprocessing, and safety steps.
pipeline.technicalNote: Media pipelines should pin model versions, prompts, parameters, assets, moderation, watermarking, and review metadata for reproducibility.

vlm.label: VLM
vlm.laymanDefinition: A model that connects visual inputs with language understanding or generation.
vlm.technicalNote: VLM workflows need image preprocessing, prompt grounding, output validation, and privacy review for uploaded visual content.

asr.label: ASR
asr.laymanDefinition: Technology that converts spoken audio into text.
asr.technicalNote: ASR systems should track language, accent, noise, timestamps, confidence, privacy, and downstream correction paths.

provenance.label: Provenance
provenance.laymanDefinition: Evidence about where media came from and how it was created or edited.
provenance.technicalNote: Provenance for generated media includes source assets, model versions, prompts, parameters, edits, disclosures, and review decisions.

questions.q: What must be true before this generated image, voice, or video reaches learners?
questions.why: Synthetic media can mislead, impersonate, bias, or violate rights even when technically impressive.

spans.text: Retrieval prompt: reconstruct responsible media by naming intent, provenance, C2PA-style credentials, consent/likeness, bias review, factual review, release log, and rollback rule.

canon_nist_genai_profile.title: NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: A course designer drops an AI-generated stock photo of a smiling "student" into a lesson thumbnail. Which risk does this raise that a generic decorative illustration would NOT?

options.text: The image may compress poorly in LMS environments.
It depicts a synthetic identity that learners may mistake for a real person, eroding trust.
Stock photos always require a paid license, unlike illustrations.
AI images load slower than vector graphics.

questions.explanation: Synthetic faces carry identity-sensitive risk because audiences can form false beliefs about real people — a concern decorative abstract imagery does not raise.

questions.prompt: A teammate exports an AI-generated audio clip and strips the file's metadata before uploading it to the asset library. What is the key accountability problem this creates?

options.text: The file will be too small to store in the library.
Visible on-screen labels are now the only disclosure, which is sufficient on its own.
Provenance — the record of how and where the asset was made — is severed, making future audits unreliable.
The audio codec becomes incompatible with most browsers.

questions.explanation: Metadata carries provenance; removing it breaks the chain of evidence that auditors and reviewers rely on, even if a visible label still appears on screen.

questions.prompt: Before publishing a lesson that features an AI-generated voice that sounds like a named public figure, name TWO preflight checks your team should complete.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Any two of: (1) confirm no real person's likeness or voice was used without consent; (2) check the training data or model card for bias risks related to the demographic represented; (3) verify a clear AI-disclosure label is attached; (4) confirm no identifiable individual can be mistaken for the synthetic speaker.
questions.explanation: Consent and bias review are the two core preflight categories for any identity-sensitive synthetic media before it goes live.

questions.prompt: You run your release-gate validator on a media asset and it throws a failure. The error log says: "disclosure_label: MISSING". What does this tell you about the asset's current state?

options.text: The asset file is corrupted and must be re-generated.
The asset passed all checks except one optional recommendation.
A required checklist field — the AI disclosure label — was never filled in, so the asset is blocked from release.
The validator cannot read the file format and needs a plugin.

questions.explanation: A missing required field in a release-gate validator is a hard block — the asset cannot proceed until that field is populated and the check is re-run.

questions.prompt: Three weeks after a lesson launches, a learner reports that an AI-generated image feels misleading. Which release-log practice gives your team the fastest, most reliable path to investigate and act?

options.text: Re-generating the image with a different prompt and swapping it silently.
Linking the user report to the original release record, reviewing the logged provenance and consent fields, then executing a documented rollback if needed.
Deleting the lesson until the complaint is resolved.
Asking the learner to submit a formal legal complaint before any review begins.

questions.explanation: Release logs connect post-launch reports to the original asset record, enabling a structured review and a controlled rollback rather than ad-hoc fixes.
